planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into strongly acidic, peaty, constantly moist bog soil topped with a sand layer, mimicking commercial cranberry bog conditions.

directions: Demoranville was released from the Rutgers P.E. Marucci Center for Blueberry and Cranberry Research breeding program in New Jersey and named in honor of Dr. Irving Demoranville, the longtime director of the University of Massachusetts Cranberry Station at East Wareham who spent decades studying cranberry variety performance on Cape Cod bogs. Like its Rutgers-bred siblings Crimson Queen and Mullica Queen, it was developed as part of a modern hybridization effort aimed at combining dependable yield with fruit quality suited to the commercial processing market rather than fresh sales. Culture follows standard cranberry bog practice: strongly acidic, sandy-peat soil kept constantly saturated (pH 4.0-5.0), full sun, and periodic sand top-dressing to control weeds and refresh the rooting surface for spreading vines. As with other named cranberry hybrids, it takes several years after planting to reach full bearing and requires a sustained cold winter dormancy, making it unsuited to warm-winter or Gulf Coast plantings.

common_name: HyRed Cranberry (University of Wisconsin High-Anthocyanin Processing Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into strongly acidic, peaty, constantly moist bog soil topped with a sand layer, mimicking commercial cranberry bog conditions.

directions: HyRed was released in 1999 from the University of Wisconsin-Madison cranberry breeding program, developed specifically for its unusually high anthocyanin content, which gives the berries a deep red color and lets it ripen earlier than most other named cultivars. Processors value it for juice and sauce production, where early, intense color matters more than the large berry size prized in fresh-market cultivars like Stevens, and it has become a standard color-focused selection on Wisconsin marshes. It requires the same demanding bog culture as every cranberry: strongly acidic, constantly moist sandy-peat soil (pH 4.0-5.0), full sun, and periodic sand top-dressing to suppress weeds and encourage new rooting along the runners. Vines need several seasons to establish before cropping heavily, and a genuine winter chill period is essential, making it unsuited to warm-winter climates.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into strongly acidic, peaty, constantly moist bog soil topped with a sand layer, mimicking commercial cranberry bog conditions.

directions: Beckwith is an older Massachusetts cranberry cultivar that was selected and grown commercially well before modern Rutgers and Wisconsin hybrids like Crimson Queen and HyRed, belonging to the same mid-twentieth-century generation of named varieties as Franklin and Pilgrim that were developed to improve on older wild bog selections such as Early Black and Howes. It has long been grown on legacy Massachusetts bogs for its dependable production, though it has been progressively displaced on new plantings by higher-yielding modern hybrids. Grow it like any cranberry, in strongly acidic (pH 4.0-5.0), constantly saturated, sandy-peat bog soil topped periodically with sand to control weeds and refresh the rooting surface for the spreading vines. It is a true cold-bog plant requiring sustained winter dormancy and several years to establish before bearing a full crop, so it is unsuited to warm-winter or Gulf Coast regions.
